prompt: You send a model the sentence `The kitchen stops taking hot food orders thirty minutes before closing.` What does the model itself receive?
hint: Read the second line `tok show` printed.

choices.text: A list of twelve numbers, the ids of the pieces it was cut into
choices.why: Right. The tokenizer replaced each piece with its id, and the ids are all the model gets.

choices.text: The seventy-one characters, one at a time
choices.why: The model never sees characters. It sees the ids of the pieces they were cut into.

choices.text: The twelve words, spelt as you typed them
choices.why: The words were turned into numbers before the model saw anything.

choices.text: A short summary of what the sentence means
choices.why: Nothing summarises the text first. It is cut into pieces and numbered, all of it.

prompt: `tok show` printed the piece `" kitchen"` with the id 10084. What exactly is in that piece?

choices.text: The word alone, since the tokenizer throws spaces away
choices.why: Spaces are kept. One of them is even a token of its own in the line of code.

choices.text: The word and the full stop that ends the sentence
choices.why: The full stop is a token of its own, id 13.

choices.text: The first three letters, with the rest in the next token
choices.why: `" kitchen"` is one piece. A word is cut only when the vocabulary has no whole piece for it.

choices.text: The word together with the space that comes in front of it
choices.why: Yes. The space before a word belongs to the token, which is why `" strawberry"` and `strawberry` are cut differently.

prompt: With `o200k_base`, `cozinha` stayed whole and `trinta` came out as `" tr"` and `"inta"`. Why?
hint: What does the vocabulary have, and what does it lack?

choices.text: The tokenizer splits every Portuguese word after its second letter
choices.why: `cozinha`, `aceitar` and `fechar` all stayed whole in the same sentence.

choices.text: `trinta` is a number word, and numbers are cut into digits
choices.why: It was cut into `tr` and `inta`, not digits. Numbers written in digits are cut in chunks of up to three.

choices.text: The vocabulary holds a piece for the first word and none for the second
choices.why: Right. A word without a token of its own is spelt from smaller pieces the vocabulary does have.

choices.text: The word was misspelt
choices.why: `trinta` is spelt correctly. It is simply not common enough in the tokenizer's training text to have a piece of its own.

prompt: `seven` is one token and `SEVEN` is two. What does that mean for the model?

choices.text: Nothing; the tokenizer lowercases text before cutting it
choices.why: It does not: the two came out with different ids and a different count.

choices.text: It sees two different sequences of numbers
choices.why: Yes. Case changes the pieces, and the model learnt about each sequence separately.

choices.text: The capital version is twice as important to it
choices.why: The number of tokens says nothing about importance. It says how the characters were cut.

choices.text: It cannot read capitals, so `SEVEN` is lost
choices.why: `SE` and `VEN` reach it like any other pieces. They are just different pieces from `seven`.

prompt: Why do tokenizers use pieces of words, rather than whole words or single letters?
hint: Think about what each alternative costs.

choices.text: Whole words would make every text longer than pieces do
choices.why: It is single letters that would make texts longer. Whole words fail because no list can contain them all.

choices.text: A list of pieces spells any text and still keeps common words to one token
choices.why: Right. Whole words cannot cover every name and typo; letters would make every text several times longer.

choices.text: Pieces of words carry more meaning than whole words, so the model understands more
choices.why: The choice is about covering any text at a sensible length, not about meaning.

choices.text: Models cannot handle a list with more than a few thousand entries
choices.why: `o200k_base` has about two hundred thousand, and the ids in the captures go past 150,000.

prompt: A customer types a brand name the tokenizer has never seen. What happens to it?
hint: Single bytes are still in the list.

choices.text: It is spelt out of smaller pieces
choices.why: Yes. Byte-pair encoding keeps the single bytes, so any text can be written; the cost is more tokens.

choices.text: It is replaced by a special token that means unknown word
choices.why: Nothing is out of vocabulary for a byte-level tokenizer. The name is spelt from smaller pieces.

choices.text: The tokenizer refuses the text and the request fails with an error
choices.why: Any text can be cut, because the vocabulary still contains every single byte.

choices.text: The tokenizer adds the name to its vocabulary for next time
choices.why: The vocabulary is fixed when the tokenizer is built. It does not grow while you use it.

prompt: The Portuguese sentence about the kitchen was 16 tokens with `o200k_base`. How many more tokens did `cl100k_base` need for it?
hint: Read the count on the last line of each.

prompt: Which of these are true of `o200k_base` and `cl100k_base`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare the two English captures line by line.

choices.text: They cut the English kitchen sentence into 12 tokens each
choices.why: Yes: twelve with each, and the same pieces.

choices.text: `o200k_base` has a vocabulary about twice the size
choices.why: Yes. The number in each name is roughly the size of the vocabulary.

choices.text: They give the same id to the same piece
choices.why: `"The"` is 976 in one and 791 in the other. An id only means something inside its own list.

choices.text: A count from either one is an estimate for a model that uses the other
choices.why: Yes, and for a model with a tokenizer of its own. That is why a count names its encoding.

prompt: Why are a model's prices and limits counted in tokens?
hint: What does the model read, and what does it write?

choices.text: Tokens are a billing unit with no connection to the work the model does
choices.why: They are the work: one output token is one step of the loop from lesson 1.

choices.text: Words vary in length, so providers picked a unit that is fairer to customers
choices.why: Fairness is not the reason, and tokens vary in length too. Tokens are what the model processes.

choices.text: Tokens are the units the model reads and writes, one step of work each
choices.why: Right. Each input token is read and each output token is one turn of the generation loop.

choices.text: Characters would be too difficult for a computer to count
choices.why: Counting characters is trivial. The model simply does not work in characters.

prompt: `hours.en.txt` is 37 words and 41 tokens; `hours.pt.txt` is 39 words and 48 tokens. You are building a product for Brazilian customers. What should you take from this?
hint: Which of the three numbers does the bill use?

choices.text: Estimate from English word counts, since two words of difference is negligible
choices.why: Two words became seven tokens, and with `cl100k_base` the gap was 17.

choices.text: Measure the token count on real Portuguese text before estimating anything
choices.why: Yes. Words and characters did not predict the difference, and a rule of thumb taken from English would underestimate it.

choices.text: Count characters, since the Portuguese file has fewer of them and so costs less
choices.why: It has fewer characters and more tokens. The bill follows the tokens.

choices.text: Translate every prompt into English first to make the cost the same
choices.why: Translation is a step that can go wrong and costs tokens too. Measure first.

prompt: In the price lists of large providers, an output token often costs several times more than an input token. What is the reason given in this lesson?
hint: Can the output tokens be produced together?

choices.text: Output comes one token at a time; input is read in one pass
choices.why: Right. Each output token depends on the one before it, so they cannot be produced together.

choices.text: Output tokens are longer pieces of text
choices.why: Both are cut by the same tokenizer. A token is the same kind of piece either way.

choices.text: Providers simply charge more for what the model says
choices.why: There is a technical reason: the input can be processed in parallel and the output cannot.

choices.text: Each output token passes a separate safety check
choices.why: Nothing in this lesson says so. The difference comes from how the two are computed.

prompt: With the illustrative prices 2 and 8 per million, ten thousand requests cost 24.96 with 300 output tokens each and 3.36 with 30. By how much did the bill fall?
hint: Subtract the second total from the first.

prompt: The tenth message in a chat costs much more input than the first, although the user typed about the same amount. Why?
hint: Lesson 2: what does the application send with each request?

choices.text: The model charges extra for remembering the earlier turns between requests
choices.why: It remembers nothing between requests. The application sends the earlier turns again, and they are counted as input.

choices.text: The provider raises the price per token after the first few messages
choices.why: The price per token did not change. The number of tokens did.

choices.text: Later replies are longer by design
choices.why: That would be output, not input. The input grew because the history is resent.

choices.text: The whole conversation so far is sent again as input
choices.why: Yes. The model keeps nothing between requests, so the earlier turns are paid for again every time.

prompt: `tok cost` takes two prices per million ___: one for input and one for output.
hint: The unit every limit and price is counted in.

prompt: A model miscounts the letter r in `strawberry`. What does `tok show` explain about that?

choices.text: The tokenizer removes repeated letters before the model reads the word
choices.why: The text is not changed, only cut into pieces and numbered.

choices.text: The word arrives as one number, with its letters inside
choices.why: Right. The three r's are not in the input; the model has only what it learnt about that token's spelling.

choices.text: Counting letters needs a bigger context window than the model has
choices.why: The question is seven tokens. The difficulty is that the letters are hidden inside one of them.

choices.text: The model was never trained on English names of fruit
choices.why: It has a whole token for `" strawberry"`, so the word was common in its training text.

prompt: You need a model to count letters in a word reliably. Which instruction turns the letters into something it can see?
hint: What would make each letter its own token?

choices.text: Spell the word out one letter per line, then count the letters
choices.why: Yes. Written out, each letter is a token of its own. A program is more reliable still.

choices.text: Write the word in capitals so that it stands out
choices.why: `SEVEN` became `SE` and `VEN`: still pieces, not letters.

choices.text: Tell the model to take extra care with spelling
choices.why: Care does not put the letters into the input. They are still hidden inside a token.

choices.text: Raise the temperature so the model explores more answers
choices.why: Temperature changes how the next token is drawn (lesson 13), not what is visible in the input.

prompt: `1234567` came out as `123`, `456` and `7`. Why does that make arithmetic harder for a model?

choices.text: The digits that must line up arrive in chunks
choices.why: Right. The units sit at the end of a chunk the other number has cut in a different place.

choices.text: The model cannot hold any number above 999
choices.why: It holds the number fine as three tokens. The problem is lining digits up across chunks.

choices.text: The tokenizer rounds large numbers before the model sees them
choices.why: Nothing is rounded: `123` `456` `7` spell the whole number.

choices.text: Numbers are removed from the input and replaced with a placeholder
choices.why: They are all there, as tokens like any others.

prompt: Put what happens to your text before a model can use it in order.
hint: It starts with what you typed.
items: The tokenizer cuts it into pieces from its vocabulary
Each piece is replaced by its id
The model receives the list of ids
